name: Volite / Volift

lead: Juvéderm Volite (also sold as Skinvive, gel VYC-12) is a crosslinked hyaluronic acid gel placed in the skin to give smoother, more hydrated, finer-textured skin, particularly on the cheeks, without adding volume. Volift is a different product in the same family, a filler for lines and folds.

The hyaluronic acid binds water in the dermis, which is meant to improve surface smoothness and hydration, and it is described as lower-concentration and longer-lasting than older boosters. Published work includes a prospective single-arm study in people with cheek roughness, a retrospective cohort, a small randomised split-face trial with botulinum toxin and several manufacturer-sponsored trials.

paras: A clinician injects small amounts of gel into the dermis at multiple points across the cheeks or other areas. It is often paired with botulinum toxin or fillers as a skin-quality step, with results assessed over the following weeks.

Reported effects are mainly injection-site swelling, redness and bruising. Hyaluronic acid fillers carry rarer risks including lumps, delayed inflammatory reactions and vascular complications. It is a regulated device administered by clinicians.

angle.text: Juvéderm Volite (VYC-12, also sold as Skinvive) is injected into the skin to leave it smoother and more hydrated rather than to add volume. The hyaluronic acid binds water in the dermis, improving surface texture. Trials exist, mostly single-arm and manufacturer-linked.

lead: Juvéderm Volite is a crosslinked hyaluronic acid (HA) gel (VYC-12, marketed in the US as Skinvive) injected into the skin, rather than under it, to improve skin quality attributes such as surface smoothness and hydration.[1][2] People seek it for a smoother, more hydrated and more luminous complexion rather than for added volume, and it is described as providing longer-lasting effects at a lower HA concentration than traditional fillers.[3][2]

In a prospective single-arm study, patients with moderate or severe cheek skin roughness received VYC-12 and the authors reported it as safe and effective for improving facial skin topography.[1] In the US, the FDA approved Skinvive on 15 May 2023 for improving cheek skin smoothness in adults over 21, on the basis of a randomized, evaluator-blinded pivotal study reported by the manufacturer.[2] Other published work includes a Brazilian retrospective cohort,[3] a randomised split-face trial combined with botulinum toxin,[4] and several registered manufacturer-sponsored trials.[5][6][7]

Volift is a separate Juvéderm product in the same Vycross family, a higher-concentration gel used for lines and folds such as the nasolabial folds and perioral region, not for skin hydration.[8][9] The two names are covered together here because they are often confused.
infobox: Single-arm, retrospective and one small randomised trial
SKINVIVE by Juvéderm, 15 May 2023 (cheek skin smoothness, adults over 21) [2]

paras: Hyaluronic acid fillers are generally crosslinked to prolong their duration.[10] Wikipedia describes Juvéderm as a hyaluronic-acid-based line approved by the FDA in 2006 for nasolabial folds and used for lips, hollows and scars, with correction usually absorbed over six to nine months.[11] Volite is positioned as a skin-quality product intended to improve texture and hydration instead of volume.[1][3]

The manufacturer describes Skinvive as an intradermal microdroplet injection of HA gel with a small amount of lidocaine, indicated for the cheeks, with an optional touch-up a month after the first session and a required provider training program before purchase.[2]

A 2015 plastic surgery review of the Vycross technology, which mixes high- and low-molecular-weight HA with enhanced crosslinking, lists Voluma at 20 mg/mL (high G prime, for vertical lift and volume), Volbella at 15 mg/mL (lower G prime, for lips and fine lines) and Volift at 17.5 mg/mL, between the two, giving subtle lift with some spread and a use in the perioral region and in fine lines.[8]

A randomized, double-blind split-face study in 48 women compared DKL23 with Juvéderm Volift for moderate-to-severe nasolabial folds. Both gels produced significant improvement on the Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale at each timepoint to nine months, with similar changes between them.[9] An Italian experience with two Vycross fillers in the perioral and lip regions has also been reported.[12] This is a different use from Volite, which targets skin quality.

The prospective single-arm VYC-12 study enrolled subjects with moderate or severe cheek skin roughness on the Allergan Skin Roughness Scale, who were treated in the cheeks and forehead and/or neck, with touch-up at 30 days and optional repeat treatment at 9 months. Of 131 subjects, 31 (23.7 percent) received touch-up. The responder rate (cheeks with at least a 1-point improvement) was 96.2 percent at month 1, 76.3 percent at month 4, 34.9 percent at month 6 and 87.1 percent after repeat treatment. Instrument-measured skin hydration improved significantly from baseline at all timepoints through month 9, and treatment-related adverse events were mild or moderate.[1]

A retrospective cohort of patients treated between 2018 and 2019 at a private clinic in Rio de Janeiro examined routine-practice use and safety.[3] A prospective study of 45 patients combined Fraxel laser, microbotox and a very low G prime HA (Volite) and reported that 98 percent showed smoother, more hydrated skin, though the combination design does not isolate the gel.[13]

The manufacturer's pivotal study for US approval was randomized, multicenter and evaluator-blinded. The company reported that 58 percent (73 of 125) of treated patients had at least a 1-point improvement on the Allergan Cheek Smoothness Scale at one month and 56 percent (69 of 124) at six months, and that patient-reported satisfaction with radiance, hydration, refreshed appearance and skin health was higher at six months than before treatment.[2]

A randomised, double-blind split-face trial in 25 women combined onabotulinumtoxinA with Volite (Skinvive) for periorbital wrinkles and assessed efficacy and durability with electromyography, the Merz scale and FACE-Q at up to six months.[4]

Registered trials include a healthy-volunteer study of skin quality attributes,[14] studies in China for neck lines (n=159) and perioral lines (n=198),[5][6] a phase 2/3 skin quality study,[7] and a phase 4 study of combined facial treatment and subject satisfaction.[15] Their outcomes have not been published.

Hyaluronic acid fillers can cause bruising, redness, pain, swelling, lumps, and rarely vascular occlusion or granulomatous reactions.[10] A 2026 computational study modelled risk of delayed immune and fibrotic reactions across 26 fillers and genotypes; it is a modelling analysis rather than a clinical trial.[16]

The manufacturer lists common reactions as redness, lumps, swelling, bruising, tenderness, pain, firmness, discoloration and itching, most mild or moderate. Its key warning is unintended injection into a blood vessel, which can cause serious and possibly permanent complications including vision changes, blindness and stroke. Contraindications include a history of multiple severe allergies or anaphylaxis and allergy to lidocaine or Gram-positive bacterial proteins, and the label advises limiting strenuous exercise, sun and heat exposure, and alcohol for 24 hours. Safety in other body areas has not been established.[2] Wikipedia notes Allergan's advice against use in patients with severe allergies and the risk of granulomas with Juvéderm products.[11]
